ai.title: Renal Vein
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The renal vein drains blood from the kidney into the inferior vena cava. Its anatomy, variants, and clinical significance—especially in thrombosis, surgery, and imaging—are crucial for ward practice.

b: Right renal vein: 6–8 cm, enters IVC at L1
Left renal vein: 12 cm, crosses aorta, receives lumbar veins
sections.p: The renal vein is a short vessel (≈6–8 cm) that carries deoxygenated blood from the kidney to the inferior vena cava (IVC). Each kidney has one renal vein; the left is longer (≈12 cm) because it must cross the aorta to reach the IVC.

b: Renal vein length difference explains left‑sided thrombosis risk
Lumbar veins and gonadal veins drain into the left renal vein
sections.p: Understanding the renal vein’s course, tributaries, and variants is essential for interpreting imaging, planning surgery, and diagnosing thrombosis.

b: Pregnancy: 1:10,000 incidence, often in the third trimester
Nephrotic syndrome: 10–20% of patients develop RVT
Malignancy: 5–10% of renal cancers cause RVT
sections.p: Renal vein thrombosis (RVT) presents with flank pain, hematuria, and hypertension. It is a surgical emergency, especially in pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome, and malignancy.

t.b: Assesses flow; absence of flow suggests thrombosis
Gold standard for RVT; shows filling defect and renal size
Screen for thrombophilias (protein C/S, antithrombin, Factor V Leiden)

b: Ask about recent pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome, or malignancy
sections.p: Examiners often ask about distinguishing RVT from other causes of flank pain and the first steps in management.

t.b: Start anticoagulation with low‑molecular‑weight heparin; consider thrombolysis if renal function deteriorates

b: Misattributing flank pain to infection without imaging
sections.p: Students confuse RVT with renal artery thrombosis or pyelonephritis. They may overlook the left‑sided predominance or the need for urgent anticoagulation.

b: Renal artery thrombosis: sudden loss of kidney perfusion, not venous congestion
sections.p: Renal artery thrombosis, pyelonephritis, and renal cell carcinoma.

b: Use repeat imaging if clinical suspicion remains high
sections.p: A normal Doppler may occur if the thrombus is small or if the patient is dehydrated. CT may miss a small thrombus if contrast timing is off.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe flank pain with hematuria and hypertension
Signs of pulmonary embolism (if RVT is extensive)
